answer.label: Not George Washington — a spurious attribution
answer.authorName: Unknown — a reworked proverb, falsely credited to Washington

answer.sourceLine: There is no record of George Washington ever writing or saying this. It surfaces only in 1902 — over 100 years after his 1799 death — and Mount Vernon lists it among its “spurious quotations.” The line is a late reworking of a centuries-old proverb (“fire is a good servant but a bad master”) with “government” swapped in.

source.excerpt: Government is not reason, it is not eloquence,—it is force! Like fire, it is a dangerous servant, and a fearful master; never for a moment should it be left to irresponsible action.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the metaphor to proverbs from 1562 (water) and the 1600s (fire) — “a good servant but a bad master” — long predating the United States.
The earliest tie to Washington is an unsigned 1902 note in The Christian Science Journal, per Quote Investigator — 103 years after his death.
Check Your Fact rates it False and notes Mount Vernon lists the line among its spurious quotations.
source.excerptNote: The fuller 1902 wording, credited only to “the first President of the United States.” The popular short form — “Government is like fire, a dangerous servant and a fearful master” — is a later condensation.

author.name: George Washington
author.heading: Why it lands on Washington
author.metaLine: 1732–1799 · First U.S. President & Continental Army commander
author.bio: George Washington commanded the Continental Army and served as the first President of the United States. Precisely because he is the archetypal Founding Father, he is one of the internet’s most common magnets for invented “wisdom” — feel-good aphorisms pinned to his name with no documentary basis. This is one of them: his estate at Mount Vernon lists it among quotations he never actually said.

misattribution.heading: A fake old, not a Founding quote
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “fake old”: a modern-sounding maxim retrofitted onto a Founding Father to borrow his authority.

items.why: No text in Washington’s hand contains it; Mount Vernon lists it among spurious quotations, and the first tie to him is an unsigned 1902 magazine note — 103 years after his death.

The “dangerous servant / fearful master” figure descends from a “good servant, bad master” proverb applied to water (1562) and fire (1600s) long before anyone applied it to government, per Quote Investigator.
The paired “government is force” idea circulated by 1890 in connection with the Kansas senator, again with no link to Washington, per Check Your Fact.

misattribution.truthLine: The metaphor is a genuine old proverb; the Washington signature was added in 1902 and is unsupported by any record.

context.heading: A proverb in a powdered wig
lead: The saying sounds like Revolutionary-era wisdom, and that is exactly why it sticks to George Washington. But its logic is borrowed from a proverbial template far older than the United States: as early as 1562 water was called “a very good servant, but… a cruel master,” and by the 1600s writers were saying “fire is a good servant but a bad master.” Preachers and essayists then slotted in whatever subject they pleased — zeal, passion, the press, money — and eventually government.

According to Quote Investigator, the first time the metaphor is tied to Washington is an unsigned 1902 note in The Christian Science Journal — 103 years after he died. No document in Washington’s own hand contains anything like it.
context.detailsSummary: The related “Government is not reason… it is force” line
detailsBody: The short “dangerous servant / fearful master” quote usually travels attached to a longer one: “Government is not reason; it is not eloquence; it is force.” That fuller version appears in the same apocryphal 1902 text. The “government is force” idea itself was in circulation by 1890, associated with Kansas Senator John James Ingalls — again, not Washington.
context.pull: The metaphor is real and old; the Washington signature is not.
